newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE - Vietnam vets finally to be welcomed home.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Vietnam vets finally to be welcomed home.

text.p: Vietnam War veterans will finally get an official welcome home parade in New Zealand -- a quarter of a century late.
Kiwi soldiers returning in the late 1960s and early 1970s were forced to keep a low profile in the face of a strong anti-war protest movement.
Parade organiser and veteran Paddy Driver, 48, says the "Vietnam Remembered" parade, planned for June 1998, will be a long-overdue welcome home.

"It was an uncomfortable feeling...When we came back you weren't exactly prepared to walk around the town with your uniform on for fear of ridicule," said Driver, who as a 20-year-old spent a year in Vietnam as an infantry soldier.

New Zealand sent troops in 1965 to support the U.S. and South Vietnamese governments in their war against communist North Vietnam. Of the 3,890 New Zealand soldiers who fought there, 37 were killed and 187 wounded.
The six-year deployment -- the longest in New Zealand's military history -- involved only 550 soldiers at its peak, but stirred strong domestic opposition.

It was the first time New Zealanders had been on the losing side in a war, and Driver said some soldiers have never been able to fully cope with the trauma of combat and their chilly reception at home.
"They were pretty young at that stage of the game. You didn't talk much about it. It's pretty important that they can talk to their mates and get it off their chests," he said.
NEED FOR COUNSELLING NOT RECOGNISED

Post-traumatic stress syndrome -- a combat-related malady marked by depression, anxiety and flashbacks -- was unrecognised at the time and counselling almost non-existent. The parade, bringing together veterans from New Zealand and overseas, was intended as part of the healing process for those still nursing psychological wounds.

"These guys went through a year with people shooting at them almost on a daily basis in some cases, and they got nothing, so there's some pretty bitter and twisted guys out there. The majority of the guys, I suspect, have probably just got on with their lives...but there are other guys who hit the old alcohol, are depressed and wandering around life," Driver said.

He said the Returned Services Associations, whose membership at the time consisted mainly of World War Two soldiers, did not always welcome Vietnam veterans. "The general feeling at the time was: 'You guys wouldn't know what war was.'"
Driver's local RSA had sent troops monthly food parcels.

"When I came back I went to go into the RSA to thank them very much for it and I couldn't even get through the front door, because I was a young fella. I tried to explain...but the guy behind the door says: 'I don't want to hear any of that crap. If you don't get out of here now, I'll call the police.'
"So that was my welcome back to New Zealand," he said.
Now a local council employee in Porirua, near Wellington, Driver hopes anti-Vietnam War sentiment has faded with time and that the public will back the parade.
Only one critical letter has landed on his desk, and he rejects its suggestion that the event will glorify war. The main aim, he says, is simply reunion.
LARGE CROWDS EXPECTED
Emotions are expected to run high as old friends meet again and Driver hopes the event will be as successful as one he attended in Sydney in the mid 1980s.
"It was amazing. I can remember walking down that street with tears in my eyes, and all the old fellas lining the streets, shaking your hand, and saying: 'Good on you (well done), Kiwi.'"

Around 3,000 veterans are expected to attend Vietnam Remembered, with up to 2,000 from Australia. Americans have expressed an interest, and veterans from South Korea, Thailand, the Philippines, and Canada will be invited.

The highlight will be a ticker-tape parade through Wellington. Also planned are 1960s theme concerts, exhibitions and a war plane fly-past. Organisers hope New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger will attend.
Driver said the parade will finally offer a chance to pay tribute to those who served their country in Vietnam, especially to those who died.
